> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

This law is independent of $y$; scalar uniqueness [F1] identifies each projection, and Cramer–Wold [F1] gives $Y_iX_i\sim N_d(\theta,\sigma^2I_d)$ independent of $Y_i$. By [F2], for every realized sample $S$, the posterior mean is $m(S)$ and the posterior covariance is $vI_d$ where $v=\sigma^2/(\sigma^2+n)$. The formula also gives $m=0,v=1$ when $n=0$. Fix $\theta,S$ with $\|m(S)\|_\infty\le\epsilon$. For a fresh test pair write $X=Y\theta+G$ with $Y$ uniform and $G\sim N_d(0,\sigma^2I_d)$ independent. Define $H(S,\theta)$ to be zero when $\|m(S)\|_\infty>\epsilon$, and otherwise to be the probability in step 1.3. For either sign $y$, $yR+G$ has law $N_d(0,(v+\sigma^2)I_d)$: each projection has the product characteristic function of independent centered scalar normals, and [F1] identifies the vector law. This conditional law is the same for both labels, so $U:=YR+G$ is independent of the uniform label. By [F6], $\mathbb P(F(S,U)\ne Y\mid S)=1/2$. The $j$th marginal odds are $L_j(+1)/L_j(-1)=((1/2+\tau)/(1/2-\tau))^{\sum_i y_ix_{ij}}$. Bayes' finite formula and [F2] give the displayed log identity. Assume $n>0$, fix $\theta$ and $j$, and put $\xi_i=\theta_jY_iX_{ij}$. By [F1], these are independent signs with mean $2\tau$. Let $t=\sqrt{2n\log(2d/\delta)}$. Since $|\sum_iY_iX_{ij}|=|\sum_i\xi_i|$, this proves $\mathbb P(|\sum_iY_iX_{ij}|>2\tau n+t\mid\Theta=\theta)\le\delta/d$. By [F4] and averaging over the finite prior, with probability at least $1-\delta$ every coordinate obeys $|\sum_iY_iX_{ij}|\le2\tau n+t$.

On the event from step 1.3, step 1.1 and step 1.2 now yield $|L_j(S)|\le5\tau(2\tau n+t)\le15\tau t$ for every $j$, which is the asserted bound. If $n=0$, the posterior equals the uniform prior, so every $L_j=0$ and the claimed bound holds with equality.

$$L_{\Delta,f}(x,y)=\sup_{x'\in\Delta(x)}\ell(f(x'),y).$$
Its robust risk is the outer expectation
$$R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P,\Delta}(f)=\mathbb E_P^*[L_{\Delta,f}(X,Y)] :=\inf\{\mathbb E_P[g(X,Y)]:g\ge L_{\Delta,f}\text{ and }g\text{ is nonnegative measurable}\}.$$
If $L_{\Delta,f}$ is measurable, this is its ordinary expectation. The supremum need not be attained. Coordinates with $w_j=0$ contribute zero. Thus the margin $M:=\sum_jw_jQ_j$ is stochastically at most $\widetilde M:=\sum_j|w_j|E_j$.

Represent each $E_j=A_j+B_j$, where $A_j$ is Bernoulli with mean $a$, $B_j=0$ if $A_j=1$, and conditional on $A_j=0$, $B_j$ is a uniform sign. Then $\mathbb E\sum_j|w_j|A_j=a\|w\|_1$. Conditional on the vector $(A_j)$, the sum $\sum_j|w_j|B_j$ is symmetric about zero, so it is nonpositive with probability at least $1/2$. The expected robust risk is therefore at least $(1-\gamma/2)(1-\gamma)/2\ge1/2-\gamma$, since the difference is $\gamma/4+\gamma^2/4\ge0$. The zero-weight and $\epsilon=0$ cases in step 5.1 satisfy the same final bound.

If $x\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ and $\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon<1$, then $x_j+\delta_j>0$ when $x_j=+1$ and $x_j+\delta_j<0$ when $x_j=-1$. By [F9], $T(x+\delta)=x$ coordinatewise. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $d,n\ge1$ be integers, let $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $\|\theta\|_2=\sqrt d$, let $\sigma>0$, and draw independent training pairs $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ from the two-class spherical Gaussian model with parameters $\theta,\sigma$. Set $W=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_iX_i$ and let $f_W(x)=+1$ when $\langle W,x\rangle\ge0$ and $f_W(x)=-1$ otherwise. For $0<\beta<1$, if
$$0\le\epsilon\le\frac{2\sqrt n-1}{2\sqrt n+4\sigma}-\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2\log(1/\beta)}}{\sqrt d},$$
then with probability at least $1-2\exp(-d/(8(\sigma^2+1)))$ over the training sample, the $\ell_\infty$ robust risk of $f_W$ under $P_{\theta,\sigma}$ at radius $\epsilon$ is at most $\beta$.

In particular, if $\sigma\le d^{1/4}/32$, then each of the following two conditions is sufficient for $\ell_\infty$ robust risk at most $1/100$ with the same training-sample probability:

- $0\le\epsilon\le(1/4)d^{-1/4}$ and $n\ge1$;
- $(1/4)d^{-1/4}\le\epsilon\le1/4$ and $n\ge64\epsilon^2\sqrt d$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $n\ge0$ be an integer, let $\sigma>0$ and $\epsilon\ge0$, draw $\Theta\sim N_d(0,I_d)$, and, conditional on $\Theta$, draw $n$ independent training pairs $S=((X_i,Y_i))_{i=1}^n$ from the two-class spherical Gaussian model with parameters $\Theta,\sigma$. Let $\mathcal S_n=(\mathbb R^d\times\{-1,+1\})^n$, and let $F:\mathcal S_n\times\mathbb R^d\to\{-1,+1\}$ be a Borel learning rule; write $f_S(x)=F(S,x)$. Define $m(S)=(\sigma^2+n)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_iX_i$, with the empty sum equal to zero. Define the expected robust risk as the outer expectation over $(\Theta,S)$ of $R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P_{\Theta,\sigma},\Delta_\epsilon}(f_S)$, using the same measurable-majorant convention as robust risk; when this random robust risk is measurable, this is its ordinary expectation. Then
$$\mathbb E^*_{\Theta,S}\!\left[R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P_{\Theta,\sigma},\Delta_\epsilon}(f_S)\right]\ge\frac12\,\mathbb P_{V\sim N_d(0,I_d)}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{\sigma^2+n}}\,\|V\|_\infty\le\epsilon\right).$$Consequently, if $d\ge2$ and $n\le\epsilon^2\sigma^2/(8\log d)$, then$$\mathbb E^*_{\Theta,S}\!\left[R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P_{\Theta,\sigma},\Delta_\epsilon}(f_S)\right]\ge\frac12\left(1-\frac1d\right).$$

For the lower bound, $\epsilon^2\sigma^2/(8\log d)=(1/16)(\sqrt d/1024)/(8\log d)=\sqrt d/(131072\log d)$. Thus the stated lower sample-size condition is exactly the premise of [F2], which gives the second assertion.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $\theta\in\{-1,+1\}^d$, and let $0<\tau\le1/2$. The $(\theta,\tau)$ binary-feature Bernoulli model is the probability law $P_{\theta,\tau}$ on $\{-1,+1\}^d\times\{-1,+1\}$ defined by
$$P_{\theta,\tau}(\{(x,y)\})=\frac12\prod_{j=1}^d\left[\left(\frac12+\tau\right)\mathbf1_{\{x_j=y\theta_j\}}+\left(\frac12-\tau\right)\mathbf1_{\{x_j=-y\theta_j\}}\right].$$
Thus $Y$ is uniform on $\{-1,+1\}$ and, conditional on $Y=y$, the feature coordinates are independent, with $X_j=y\theta_j$ with probability $1/2+\tau$ and $X_j=-y\theta_j$ with probability $1/2-\tau$. The displayed masses sum to one because each coordinate factor sums to one over its two possible signs and the label weights sum to one. The uniform-prior experiment used below draws $\Theta$ uniformly from $\{-1,+1\}^d$ and then draws observations conditionally independently from $P_{\Theta,\tau}$.

Input: an integer $d\ge1$ and a vector $x\in\mathbb R^d$. Output $T(x)\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ with
$$T(x)_i= \begin{cases} +1,&x_i\ge0,\\ -1,&x_i<0 \end{cases} \qquad (1\le i\le d).$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\Sigma_Y)$ be measurable spaces, let $\mathcal A$ be a measurable action space, and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. A threat correspondence is a map $\Delta:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ with $\Delta(x)\ne\varnothing$ for every $x$. It is measurable when its graph $\{(x,x')\in\mathcal X^2:x'\in\Delta(x)\}$ belongs to $\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_X$. For a measurable predictor $f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal A$ and a nonnegative measurable loss $\ell:\mathcal A\times\mathcal Y\to[0,+\infty]$, the pointwise robust loss is
$$L_{\Delta,f}(x,y)=\sup_{x'\in\Delta(x)}\ell(f(x'),y).$$
Its robust risk is the outer expectation
$$R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P,\Delta}(f)=\mathbb E_P^*[L_{\Delta,f}(X,Y)] :=\inf\{\mathbb E_P[g(X,Y)]:g\ge L_{\Delta,f}\text{ and }g\text{ is nonnegative measurable}\}.$$
If $L_{\Delta,f}$ is measurable, this is its ordinary expectation. The supremum need not be attained. For a metric $\rho$ on $\mathcal X$ and a radius $\epsilon\ge0$, the closed-ball threat is $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x'\in\mathcal X:\rho(x,x')\le\epsilon\}$. On $\mathbb R^d$, $\|u\|_\infty:=\max_{1\le j\le d}|u_j|$ and the $\ell_\infty$ threat is $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x+\delta:\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$. For a binary classifier $f:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$, the robust zero-one loss is $\mathbf1\{\exists x'\in\Delta_\epsilon(x):f(x')\ne y\}$.

For $w\in\mathbb R^d$, let $f_w(x)=+1$ when $\langle w,x\rangle\ge0$ and $f_w(x)=-1$ otherwise. In the following lower-bound branch, let $d\ge1$, $0<\tau\le1/4$, $0<\gamma<1/2$, and $0\le\epsilon<3\tau$. Draw $\Theta$ uniformly from $\{-1,+1\}^d$ and, conditional on $\Theta$, draw $n\ge0$ independent training observations $S$ from the binary-feature Bernoulli model with parameters $\Theta,\tau$. Let $g_n$ be any function from the finite sample space to $\mathbb R^d$, set $w=g_n(S)$, and use $f_w$. If
$$n\le\frac{\epsilon^2\gamma^2}{5000\tau^4\log(4d/\gamma)},$$
then the expected robust risk for the closed threat $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x+\delta:\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$ of $f_w$, averaged over $\Theta,S$, and a fresh test pair from $P_{\Theta,\tau}$, is at least $1/2-\gamma$.

In the separate thresholded upper-bound branch, let $d\ge1$, $0<\tau\le1/2$, $0<\beta<1$, and let $\theta\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ satisfy $\tau\ge(\log(1/\beta)/(2d))^{1/4}$. Draw one training pair $(X_0,Y_0)$ from $P_{\theta,\tau}$, set $W=Y_0X_0$, and define $T:\mathbb R^d\to\{-1,+1\}^d$ by $T(x)_j=+1$ when $x_j\ge0$ and $T(x)_j=-1$ otherwise. Then for every $0\le\epsilon<1$, with training-sample probability at least $1-e^{-\tau^2d/2}$, the robust risk for the closed threat $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x+\delta:\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$ of $f_W\circ T$ under $P_{\theta,\tau}$ is at most $\beta$.

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ and any $\delta$ with $\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon<1$. If $x_j=+1$, then $x_j+\delta_j\ge1-\epsilon>0$, so [F2] gives $T(x+\delta)_j=+1=x_j$. If $x_j=-1$, then $x_j+\delta_j\le-1+\epsilon<0$, so $T(x+\delta)_j=-1=x_j$. Hence $T(x+\delta)=x$ for every admissible perturbation.

For each support point $(x,y)$, every allowed perturbation therefore makes $g(T(x+\delta))=g(x)$. The robust zero-one loss of $g\circ T$ equals $\mathbf1\{g(x)\ne y\}$ pointwise. Taking expectation under $P_{\theta,\tau}$ proves the displayed equality.

Under the final $\tau,\beta$ condition, [F4] gives the one-sample risk bound for $f_{Y_0X_0}\circ T$ with the stated probability. The pointwise identity in step 2.1 explains why every radius $\epsilon<1$ has the same risk.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
